% Do not edit by hand; modify papers/f2_methodology.md and re-run the script.



The standard practice for evaluating training-recipe interventions (RmsNorm,
weight decay, dropout, label smoothing, gradient clipping, warmup schedules,
latent clamping) in transformer language models is multi-seed mean BPB
comparison, sometimes supplemented with Cohen's \emph{d} or paired t-tests. We
show that this practice systematically misattributes effects when one
intervention (commonly weight decay) acts as a strong mediator for another.

We introduce a Pearl-style controlled-direct-effect (CDE) framework
operationalized through three contributions: (1) a stratification mechanism
(\texttt{Stratum::Wd0}, \texttt{Stratum::Warmup0}) that pins a candidate mediator to its
disabled value while sweeping the remaining ablation space; (2) a four-path
Daniel et al. decomposition with multivariate delta-method standard errors,
yielding per-path 95\% CIs valid at N=5 seeds; (3) an additive bridge-score
sensitivity envelope (Ohnishi \& Li 2026, Thm 2) that translates CI bounds
into VanderWeele-Ding tipping points across an outcome-residual grid.

Applied to a sandbox-scale (~8K params, 200 steps, 5 seeds) ablation
matrix, the framework reveals a \textbf{sign flip in the intervention's direction of effect}: under canonical mediation, the Natural Direct
Effect (NDE) of replacing RmsNorm with LayerNorm is $-$4.12 BPB
(the replacement helps --- BPB drops by 4.12), but under wd=0 Pearl
CDE the same estimand is \textbf{+0.43 BPB [+0.01, +0.84]} (the
replacement hurts --- BPB rises by 0.43 --- and the 95\% CI excludes
zero). We frame this as a unit-test
demonstration on a synthetic task that the framework detects a sign
flip when one is constructed --- the magnitudes are sandbox-specific
and we do not claim the qualitative finding transfers to
champion-scale models without additional evidence; champion-scale
validation is pre-registered in \texttt{docs/F2\_PRE\_REG.md}. A
swap-parameterization Phase 0 run (committed at \texttt{data/loop49\_swap/})
confirms a narrower secondary finding: under (`M\_1 = rms, M\_2 =
warmup`), the rms-mediated Natural Indirect Effect (NIE) of weight
decay is \textbf{byte-identical $-$0.751 [$-$1.325, $-$0.177] BPB across all three strata} --- the only path-specific effect (PSE) row in our
matrix that survives intact across canonical, wd0, and warmup0
reference points.

The framework is open-source in Rust with 10 binaries, 830
unit/integration tests, and W3C-PROV-tagged CSV provenance
preambles. We release it as a reproducibility artifact for ML
methodology research.



\section{Introduction}\label{sec:1}



\subsection{The problem with seed-mean ablation}\label{sec:1.1}


The median ML ablation report follows a fixed recipe: pick a target
intervention \texttt{X}, train \texttt{N in \{3, 5\}} seeds with and without \texttt{X},
report \texttt{Δ +/- sigma/√N} on a held-out metric, and infer that \texttt{X} helps,
hurts, or is null. This recipe is statistically defensible when every
other configuration parameter is held fixed, but ML training recipes
are not single-knob systems. A transformer training run simultaneously
exercises weight decay, learning-rate warmup, gradient clipping,
RmsNorm vs LayerNorm, label smoothing, and dropout --- to name only the
canonical seven we ablate in \cref{sec:4}. Two of these knobs are statistically
dependent whenever one is on the regularization path of the other.

When such a dependency exists, a seed-mean ablation reports the
\textbf{marginal} effect of \texttt{X}: the average over the empirical joint of all
other knobs in the training configuration. The marginal effect is what
practitioners actually consume --- "should I turn this on by default?" ---
but it is silent on a more dangerous failure mode: \textbf{suppression mediation}, where one intervention's effect is dominated by its
correlated mediator, and the apparent sign of the effect flips when the
mediator is held at a non-default reference value. Our empirical
demonstration in \cref{sec:5} documents this failure mode in two layers. \textbf{First, the suppression structure is uniform across our entire ablation column}:
all five non-mediator fixes (rms, dropout, gradclip, clamp, smooth) show
canonical NDE $\approx$ $-$4.5 to $-$4.9 BPB with NIE\_M1 $\approx$ +4.5 to +5.0 BPB nearly
cancelling --- a textbook signature of dominant mediator structure.
\textbf{Second, RmsNorm is the only fix whose wd0 Pearl CDE crosses zero}:
under wd=0, every fix's NDE attenuates by roughly 10--15$\times$ (the wd0
stratum is a structural attenuator on the entire NDE column), but only
RmsNorm overshoots into positive territory --- marginal NDE $-$4.12 BPB at
canonical training becomes Pearl CDE +0.43 BPB [+0.01, +0.84] under
wd=0. Both CIs exclude zero. The sign is not a seed artifact. The
uniformity of the suppression structure is, in our view, the more
robust methodological finding; the RmsNorm sign flip is the sharpest
single instance of it.

If suppression mediation is more common than the current ablation
literature acknowledges, then a meaningful fraction of "ablation shows
\texttt{X} helps" claims may be confounded by mediators outside the
ablation. The contribution of this paper is twofold: (i) provide the
methodological and software infrastructure to detect such cases at the
same engineering cost as a normal ablation sweep, and (ii) document
one verified instance as proof-of-concept.


\subsection{Contributions}\label{sec:1.2}


\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Stratification framework}. The `Stratum::{Canonical, Wd0, Warmup0}` registry (\cref{sec:3.1}) routes a single ablation sweep across one marginal stratum and two Pearl-CDE strata, deriving the mode-string matrix from \texttt{Stratum x ModeKind} automatically so that adding a new stratum is a single-variant code change.
\item \textbf{Daniel et al. 4-PSE decomposition with finite-sample CIs}. We implement the four-path decomposition (\cref{sec:3.2}, no-interaction special case of Gao-Li-Luo 2020) with delta-method standard errors in the spirit of the Miles-Shpitser (2017) efficient-influence-function treatment (extended from their single-pathway PSE setting to the two-mediator decomposition), and we default to Student-\texttt{t} CIs at \texttt{df = 4} for the \texttt{N = 5} seed regime --- not the asymptotic \texttt{z} interval that Owen (2025) shows to undercover at that sample size.
\item \textbf{Bridge-score sensitivity envelope}. We adopt the Ohnishi-Li (2026) additive bridge-score envelope on each PSE (\cref{sec:3.3}), classifying every effect as fragile / moderate / robust against the VanderWeele-Ding tipping-point thresholds (\texttt{Γ < 1.25}, \texttt{Γ >= 2.0}).
\item \textbf{Cross-stratum stability comparator}. \texttt{f2\_stratum\_compare} (\cref{sec:3.4}) takes the three single-stratum CSVs and emits a \texttt{stable\_across\_strata} flag per PSE based on CI overlap, surfacing suppression mediation without a-priori knowledge of which mediator is doing the suppressing.
\item \textbf{Sandbox empirical demonstration with two findings}. \cref{sec:5} documents the RmsNorm $\times$ WD sign-flip at small scale (5 seeds, ~minute-of-compute per run) as a unit-test demonstration that the framework detects a sign flip when one is constructed. A narrower secondary finding from the Phase 0 swap-parameterization run (committed at \texttt{data/loop49\_swap/}): the rms-mediated indirect effect of weight decay is byte-identical across all three strata. \cref{sec:6} demonstrates that no choice in \cref{sec:3} --- point estimator, CI method, bridge-score \texttt{Λ}, stratum reference value --- flips the qualitative conclusion of either finding.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Background}\label{sec:2}



\subsection{Pearl causal mediation}\label{sec:2.1}


Under Pearl's potential-outcomes calculus, the total effect of an
intervention \texttt{X} on an outcome \texttt{Y} admits two decompositions of
practical interest in ablation work. The \textbf{natural direct-and-indirect effect (NDE/NIE)} decomposition splits the total effect into the part
that flows through a mediator \texttt{M} under its natural distribution (the
NIE) and the part that does not (the NDE). The NDE is contrastive at
the population mean of \texttt{M}, which means it answers the marginal-
ablation question --- what would change on average if I removed \texttt{X} but
left \texttt{M} to find its own equilibrium? The \textbf{controlled direct effect (CDE)} instead fixes \texttt{M} at a specific reference value \texttt{m*} and reports
the effect of \texttt{X} with \texttt{M} clamped at \texttt{m*}. The CDE answers the
counterfactual-ablation question: what would change if I removed \texttt{X}
and also disabled \texttt{M}?

When two mediators are present, Gao, Li \& Luo (2020,
\citep{arxiv:2007.16031}) develop an interaction-effect framework whose
no-interaction special case yields a four-path decomposition
additively separating the total effect into the direct effect plus
three indirect effects: through \texttt{M\_1} alone, through \texttt{M\_2} alone,
and through the sequential chain \texttt{M\_1 -> M\_2}. F2 (\cref{sec:3.2}) operates
in that no-interaction regime, with delta-method standard errors at
\texttt{N = 5} seeds derived in the spirit of the Miles-Shpitser
(2017, \citep{arxiv:1710.02011}) efficient-influence-function treatment
(originally for single-pathway PSEs with mediator-outcome
confounding; we extend the EIF logic to the two-mediator
no-interaction setting).


\subsection{Sensitivity analysis}\label{sec:2.2}


Causal estimates from observational or pseudo-observational data are
vulnerable to unmeasured confounding. The two standard formal tools
for bounding this exposure are the \textbf{E-value} of VanderWeele \& Ding
(2017, "Sensitivity Analysis in Observational Research: Introducing
the E-Value", \emph{Annals of Internal Medicine}) and the additive
\textbf{bridge-score envelope} of Ohnishi \& Li (2026, \citep{arxiv:2605.18724},
Theorem 2). The E-value quantifies the smallest confounding strength
\texttt{Γ} on the risk-ratio scale that would explain away an observed effect;
the bridge-score envelope translates the same idea to an additive
metric scale and parameterizes the envelope by a pair \texttt{(Γ, Λ)} of
sensitivity dials.

Bits-per-byte is on the additive scale by construction, so F2 (\cref{sec:3.3})
uses the bridge-score envelope directly without any log or risk-ratio
translation. We classify every PSE estimate against the
VanderWeele-Ding tipping-point thresholds (\texttt{Γ\_tip < 1.25} is fragile;
\texttt{Γ\_tip >= 2.0} is robust), which keeps the sensitivity analysis on the
same scale as the headline numbers and avoids a category mismatch
between the estimate and its sensitivity envelope.


\subsection{ML ablation practice}\label{sec:2.3}


\textbf{AblationBench} (Abramovich \& Chechik, 2025, \citep{arxiv:2507.08038},
"Evaluating Automated Planning of Ablations in Empirical AI
Research") is the closest \emph{evaluation} benchmark on the
ML-ablation methodology side. AblationBench studies whether
language-model agents can \emph{plan} the right ablations for a paper
(their best system identifies only 38\% of original ablations on
average); F2 is orthogonal to this question --- assuming the
ablation matrix is already chosen, we ask how to analyze the
resulting per-seed BPB measurements without misattributing
effects to mediator-confounded knobs.

\textbf{Benchmarking Optimizers for LLM Pretraining} (Semenov,
Pagliardini \& Jaggi, 2025, \citep{arxiv:2509.01440}) is the closest
empirical-methodology neighbour on the optimizer side: a
head-to-head benchmark of AdamW, Muon, D-Muon, SOAP, Sophia, Lion,
MARS, and AdEMAMix at multiple model sizes with 5-seed standard-
deviation reporting. F2 shares the multi-seed reporting discipline
but addresses a different inferential layer: Semenov-Pagliardini-
Jaggi report headline rankings under controlled budgets, while F2
asks which interventions in a \emph{fixed-optimizer} recipe mediate
others' BPB effects. The two analyses compose --- a paper using
either methodology in isolation answers a strict subset of the
questions a paper using both can answer.

\textbf{ABLATOR} (Fostiropoulos \& Itti, 2023) is the closest
infrastructure work --- a tool for running multi-seed ablation
studies at scale with result aggregation --- but stops at multi-seed
ranking without mediation decomposition or stratified CDE.

\textbf{A Sober Look at Progress in Language Model Reasoning}
(Hochlehnert, Bhatnagar, Udandarao, Albanie, Prabhu \& Bethge, 2025,
\citep{arxiv:2504.07086}, COLM 2025) audits the seed-, decoding-, and
hardware-sensitivity of recent LM benchmarks and argues for
standardized reporting protocols. F2's per-seed BPB measurements
with explicit MC error bars (\cref{sec:3.5.2}) and W3C-PROV-tagged CSV
preambles (\cref{sec:3.5.1}) directly operationalize two of the "sober look"
recommendations: every reported delta carries its measurement
uncertainty, and every CSV record carries enough provenance to
re-run the same recipe to the same numbers on a different machine.

A representative median-practice analysis pipeline in recent
ablation papers combines a wide-form CSV table (one row per
config $\times$ seed-summary statistic) with paired Welch t-tests and
Cohen's \texttt{d} standardized effect sizes. F2 generalizes the schema
to long-form with W3C-PROV preambles (\cref{sec:3.5.1}) and replaces paired
Welch with stratified Pearl-CDE + bridge-score sensitivity.

A parallel line of causal-mediation work in ML interpretability is
typified by \textbf{ROME} (Meng et al., 2022) and \textbf{activation patching}
(Wang et al., 2023): both apply causal-mediation language at a single
forward pass to localize knowledge or attention behaviors inside an
already-trained model. F2 targets the orthogonal question of training-
recipe mediation: which training-time interventions confound which
others. The forward-pass and training-recipe questions share a
methodological vocabulary but do not share a problem.



\section{The F2 framework}\label{sec:3}



\subsection{Stratification mechanism}\label{sec:3.1}


Let \texttt{X} denote a training-recipe intervention (one of the seven canonical
fixes: rms, warmup, gradclip, clamp, smooth, wd, dropout). Let \texttt{M subseteq \{X\}\^\{\}c}
denote a candidate mediator subset. Let \texttt{Y} denote validation BPB.

We define a \textbf{stratum} as a setting of one or more mediators to a fixed
reference value (typically "disabled"). The framework currently supports
three strata, encoded as the enum \texttt{race::ablation::Stratum}:

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
Stratum & Reference levels held fixed \\
\midrule
\texttt{Canonical} & None (free baseline, default WD=0.1) \\
\texttt{Wd0} & weight\_decay = 0.0 (Pearl CDE on WD) \\
\texttt{Warmup0} & warmup\_steps\_unquantized = 0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


Each stratum carries a CSV mode-column prefix via \texttt{Stratum::prefix()}
(empty for \texttt{Canonical}, \texttt{"wd0\_"} for \texttt{Wd0}, \texttt{"warmup0\_"} for \texttt{Warmup0}).
The cross-product with \texttt{ModeKind in \{Loco, Pairwise, Triplet\}} yields the
nine mode strings that tag every emitted row. Figure 1 visualizes the flow.

Adding a fourth stratum is a single-variant code change in
\texttt{src/race/ablation.rs}; the mode-string registry then auto-extends every
downstream lookup. The policy for when a new stratum is warranted ($\geq$50\%
indirect effect in a prior mediation analysis, plus the Pearl CDE at the
disabled value being the natural next analytical question) is documented
in the enum doc-comment.

\textbf{Figure 1}: Stratum enum + registry flow.


\subsection{Four-path decomposition for two ordered mediators}\label{sec:3.2}


Following Daniel, De Stavola, Cousens \& Vansteelandt (2015,
\emph{Biometrics} 71:1--14, doi:10.1111/biom.12248,
"Causal mediation analysis with multiple mediators"), the total
effect of \texttt{X} on \texttt{Y} in the presence of two ordered mediators
\texttt{M\_1}, \texttt{M\_2} decomposes additively into four path-specific effects
(PSEs):

$$
\text{TE}(X) \;=\; \text{NDE}(X) \;+\; \text{NIE}_{M_1}(X) \;+\; \text{NIE}_{M_2}(X) \;+\; \text{NIE}_{\text{chain}}(X)
$$

The four components are: the \textbf{natural direct effect} (the part of
\texttt{Δ Y} that does not flow through either mediator), the \textbf{natural indirect effect through \texttt{M\_1} alone}, the \textbf{natural indirect effect through \texttt{M\_2} alone}, and the \textbf{natural indirect effect through the chain \texttt{M\_1 -> M\_2}} (the path that traverses both mediators
sequentially). The Daniel et al. nested-counterfactual identification
formulas decompose the joint NIE into exactly these four pieces; the
broader interaction-effect framework of Gao, Li \& Luo (2020,
\citep{arxiv:2007.16031}, "Decomposition of the Total Effect for Two Mediators:
A Natural Counterfactual Interaction Effect Framework") supplies the
companion no-interaction reduction we adopt below --- under
no exposure-mediator interaction, every Gao-Li-Luo interaction term
vanishes and the residual decomposition collapses onto the Daniel et
al. four-PSE form.

Under \textbf{sequential ignorability} (Imai, Keele \& Tingley 2010,
\emph{Psychological Methods} 15(4): 309--334: the standard mediation-
identifying assumption that no unmeasured confounders affect both
the mediator and the outcome, conditional on the exposure) and no
exposure-mediator interaction, each PSE is identified by the
\textbf{counterfactual difference}

$$
\Delta_S \;\equiv\; \mathbb{E}\!\left[Y(\text{remove } S)\right] - \mathbb{E}\!\left[Y(\text{full stack})\right]
$$

for every \texttt{S subseteq \{X, M\_1, M\_2\}}. This \texttt{Δ\_S} notation is the
computational representation we use in \texttt{f2\_dual\_mediation}; it is
algebraically equivalent to the Daniel et al. nested-counterfactual
expressions under no-interaction, with the four-PSE decomposition:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{NDE} &= \Delta_{X, M_1, M_2} \\
\text{NIE}_{\text{chain}} &= (\Delta_X - \Delta_{X, M_1}) - (\Delta_{X, M_2} - \Delta_{X, M_1, M_2}) \\
\text{NIE}_{M_1} &= \Delta_{X, M_2} - \Delta_{X, M_1, M_2} \\
\text{NIE}_{M_2} &= \Delta_{X, M_1} - \Delta_{X, M_1, M_2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The lock test
\texttt{dual\_mediation\_no\_interaction\_residual\_lock} (\cref{sec:8.2}) certifies the
equivalence numerically: the residual
\texttt{Δ\_X − (NDE + NIE\_\{M\_1\} + NIE\_\{M\_2\} + NIE\_\{chain\})} is below
$1 \times 10^{-6}$ in our regime, which empirically confirms the no-interaction
collapse.

In our setting, \texttt{Δ\_S} is estimated per seed \texttt{i in \{1, ..., N\}} as the
within-seed difference $Y_i(\text{remove } S) - Y_i(\text{full stack})$. Each
PSE then has a per-seed estimator that is a \textbf{linear combination} of these
seed-level differences. Linearity is the crucial property: the multivariate
delta-method then reduces to the \textbf{sample variance of per-seed PSE values}. This finite-sample treatment is in the spirit of the
single-pathway efficient-influence-function derivation of Miles,
Shpitser, Kanki, Meloni \& Tchetgen Tchetgen (2017, \citep{arxiv:1710.02011},
"On semiparametric estimation of a path-specific effect in the
presence of mediator-outcome confounding"); we adapt the EIF logic
from their one-mediator setting to our two-mediator no-interaction
decomposition. The resulting per-PSE variance is:

$$
\widehat{\text{Var}}(\widehat{\text{PSE}}) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i=1}^N \left(\text{PSE}_i - \overline{\text{PSE}}\right)^2
$$

We report $\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}}$ for each PSE.

For confidence intervals at small \texttt{N}, we use the Student-t critical value
\texttt{t\_\{0.975, N-1\}}:

$$
\text{CI}_{95\%}(\widehat{\text{PSE}}) \;=\; \widehat{\text{PSE}} \;\pm\; t_{0.975, N-1} \cdot \text{SE}
$$

At $N = 5$, $t_{0.975, 4} \approx 2.776$. We deliberately avoid BCa bootstrap:
Owen (2025, \citep{arxiv:2508.10083}, "Better bootstrap-t confidence intervals
for the mean") motivates skepticism of BCa at small N by proposing a
Beta-weighted bootstrap alternative; the empirical small-N coverage
deficits of BCa it documents (as the baseline that motivates the new
method) are the relevant evidence for our purposes. The Student-t
adjustment we use is more conservative but does not require simulation
calibration, which is desirable at the demonstration scale of \cref{sec:5}.

\textbf{Implementation}: \texttt{src/bin/f2\_dual\_mediation.rs}. The
no-interaction equivalence and the residual lock test are described
above in the four-PSE block.


\subsection{Bridge-score sensitivity envelope}\label{sec:3.3}


Sequential ignorability is the identifying assumption; it may fail in the
presence of unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding. The \textbf{additive bridge-score envelope} (Ohnishi \& Li 2026, \citep{arxiv:2605.18724}, Theorem 2)
provides a sharp bound. In their notation the envelope is parameterized
by \texttt{(gamma\_a, eta\_a)}; we work with a uniform-scalar reduction
\texttt{Γ := sup\_\{m,b\} gamma\_a(m,b)}, \texttt{Λ := sup\_\{m,b\} eta\_a(m,b)} so that the
envelope can be reported per-PSE with two interpretable quantities:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{$\Gamma$ $\geq$ 1}: residual selection ratio. \texttt{Γ = 1} corresponds to no unmeasured confounding; \texttt{Γ = 2} to a doubling of the selection odds. This is the same scale family as the VanderWeele-Ding E-value, but the Ohnishi-Li bridge-conditional \texttt{gamma\_a} is provably $\leq$ the VW-D E-value (Ohnishi-Li Prop. 2), so a \texttt{Γ\_tip} reported here is a conservative-leaning analogue of the standard E-value.
\item \textbf{$\Lambda$ $\geq$ 0}: outcome scale residual (units of BPB in our setting). It bounds the maximum gap in \texttt{Y} that an unobserved confounder can induce between mediator strata.
\end{itemize}

The envelope \textbf{additively expands} the PSE confidence interval by

$$
\text{expansion}(\Gamma, \Lambda) \;=\; \Lambda \cdot \frac{\Gamma - 1}{\Gamma}
$$

(equivalent to Ohnishi-Li Theorem 2, Eq. (5), under the BPB additive
scale and the uniform-scalar reduction above). The worst-case envelope
is

$$
[\text{CI}_{\text{lo}} - \text{expansion}, \;\; \text{CI}_{\text{hi}} + \text{expansion}]
$$

A PSE \textbf{survives at zero} iff this envelope still excludes zero.

\textbf{Tipping point.} Inverting the envelope equation yields the minimum \texttt{Γ}
at which the envelope first reaches zero from the closer-to-zero CI
endpoint:

$$
\Gamma_{\text{tip}}(\Lambda) \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{\min(|\text{CI}_{\text{lo}}|, |\text{CI}_{\text{hi}}|)}{\Lambda}
$$

\texttt{Γ\_tip(Λ) -> inf} as \texttt{Λ -> 0} and \texttt{Γ\_tip(Λ) -> 1} as \texttt{Λ -> inf}. We adopt the
following thresholds \textbf{as a paper-specific reporting convention},
calibrated against the E-value literature (VanderWeele \& Ding 2017,
\emph{Annals of Internal Medicine}, and the JAMA Guide to Statistics and
Methods entry by Haneuse, VanderWeele \& Arterburn 2019). Neither paper
prescribes universal cutoffs; the tiers below are a reporting
convenience and should not be over-interpreted as the literature
consensus.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
\texttt{Γ\_tip} range & Our reporting tier \\
\midrule
\texttt{< 1.25} & \textbf{fragile}: small unmeasured confounding can flip the verdict \\
\texttt{1.25 <= x < 2} & \textbf{moderate} \\
\texttt{>= 2.0} & \textbf{robust}: requires a substantial confounder to overturn \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


The $\Lambda$-sweep emits a per-PSE $\times$ per-$\Lambda$ table in either long-form (CMAverse
convention, one row per PSE $\times$ $\Lambda$ tuple) or wide-form (one row per PSE,
columns indexed by $\Lambda$). Figure 2 visualizes the hyperbolae for rms PSEs.

\textbf{Implementation}: \texttt{src/bin/f2\_mediation\_sensitivity.rs}. The lock test
\texttt{tipping\_point\_matches\_closer\_endpoint\_over\_lambda} validates the
closed-form against a worked example.


\subsection{Cross-stratum comparator}\label{sec:3.4}


Given dual\_mediation CSVs from two or more strata, the comparator joins
rows by \texttt{(fix\_x, pse\_name)} and emits a side-by-side table with one
column triple per stratum (\texttt{estimate}, \texttt{ci95\_lo}, \texttt{ci95\_hi}). Missing
strata produce \texttt{NaN} in their slots --- explicitly, not silently --- so the
analyst sees the coverage at a glance.

The \texttt{stable\_across\_strata} flag is \texttt{true} iff every pair of present 95\%
CIs has non-empty intersection:

$$
\text{stable} \;\iff\; \forall \, i \neq j \,:\, \text{CI}^{(i)}_{\text{lo}} \le \text{CI}^{(j)}_{\text{hi}} \;\wedge\; \text{CI}^{(j)}_{\text{lo}} \le \text{CI}^{(i)}_{\text{hi}}
$$

A \texttt{false} verdict for a PSE that the analyst expected to be stratum-invariant
is a flag for further investigation: either the PSE truly differs across
strata (the sign-flip case in \cref{sec:5.2}), or one stratum's CSV is corrupted
(provenance check catches the latter).

\textbf{Implementation}: \texttt{src/bin/f2\_stratum\_compare.rs}.


\subsection{Provenance and reproducibility}\label{sec:3.5}


Statistical-causal results are only as credible as the data lineage that
produced them. Three Loop-32 audit incidents motivated a defensive provenance
discipline that is now part of the framework's binary contract:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Identical-hash divergence}. The same \texttt{config\_fingerprint} produced LOCO\_wd estimates of 0.07 BPB on one run and 0.58 BPB on a later run --- an 8$\times$ shift at a byte-identical input. Investigation revealed an uncommitted refactor of \texttt{src/transformer.rs} (the forward kernel) that changed the integration of the model but not any field hashed into \texttt{config\_fingerprint}.
\item \textbf{Silent provenance loss}. CSVs produced by older runs of \texttt{f2\_ablation\_sweep} carried no information about which trainer-internals version produced them. The hash matched; the BPB did not.
\item \textbf{Silent stratum loss}. When \texttt{f2\_dual\_mediation} consumes a stratified CSV, the resulting PSE labels (NDE, NIE\_M1, \dots{}) read like \emph{marginal} effects but are actually \textbf{Pearl CDEs}. Without a stratum tag in the output, downstream tooling cannot distinguish.
\end{enumerate}

The three defensive mechanisms below address each incident in turn.


\subsubsection{Provenance preamble (\texttt{\# prov:*} lines)}\label{sec:3.5.1}

Every CSV emitted by
\texttt{f2\_ablation\_sweep} carries a W3C-PROV / Workflow Run RO-Crate
preamble (\citep{arxiv:2312.07852}) of the form:

\begin{verbatim}
# prov:generatedAt = 1717205400 (unix seconds UTC)
# prov:wasGeneratedBy = f2_ablation_sweep --mode wd_stratified --steps 200
# prov:agent_git_sha = ae48fd5
# prov:host = host.example
# prov:trainer_internals_schema = trainer_internals_v1_2026_06_01
# prov:cargo_pkg_version = 0.1.0
\end{verbatim}

The \texttt{f2\_provenance\_check} binary validates each field with \texttt{PASS} / \texttt{WARN} /
\texttt{FAIL} exit codes (0 / 1 / 2 respectively). Schema mismatch is \texttt{FAIL}: the
binary refuses to vouch for results produced by a different trainer-internals
version. Git SHA mismatch is \texttt{WARN}: an older commit may still be valid, but
the analyst must confirm.


\subsubsection{Trainer-internals schema (\texttt{TRAINER\_INTERNALS\_SCHEMA})}\label{sec:3.5.2}

The
incident in \cref{sec:3.5.1} (1) motivated a manual integrity lock: a single string
constant in \texttt{src/race/multi\_seed.rs} that is mixed into \texttt{config\_fingerprint}.
The convention is:

> Bump \texttt{TRAINER\_INTERNALS\_SCHEMA} (e.g. \texttt{v1\_2026\_06\_01 -> v2\_2026\_06\_15})
> whenever any of the following changes: LCG seed constants, embedding/
> Xavier/Kaiming initializers, optimizer step ordering, forward or backward
> kernels, \texttt{cross\_entropy\_loss} numerics, BPB computation, or eval
> tokenization.

A lib test (\texttt{trainer\_internals\_schema\_is\_load\_bearing}) verifies
that mutating the constant changes the fingerprint output, so an
intentional bump is detectable from CI. A mtime-drift advisory
compares the schema-string date against the on-disk mtime of
\texttt{src/transformer.rs} and surfaces a stale-schema warning during
\texttt{cargo test --lib}.


\subsubsection{Stratum context propagation (\texttt{\# INPUT STRATUM = ...})}\label{sec:3.5.3}

When
\texttt{f2\_dual\_mediation} consumes a stratified CSV, it detects the row-prefix
distribution (\texttt{canonical}, \texttt{wd0}, \texttt{warmup0}, or \texttt{mixed}) and emits a
single-line stratum banner before its column header. \texttt{f2\_mediation\_sensitivity}
reads this banner from its dual\_mediation input and re-emits it in its own
output, so the stratum context survives every downstream pipeline step:

\begin{verbatim}
sweep CSV --> f2_dual_mediation --> dual CSV --> f2_mediation_sensitivity --> sens CSV
              (# INPUT STRATUM)                  (# INPUT STRATUM)
\end{verbatim}

If a stratified CSV's PSE values are mis-interpreted as marginal effects,
the banner makes the error visible at the first line of any downstream
report. The \texttt{mixed} value is itself a signal: a CSV that concatenates rows
from multiple strata is causally undefined, and the binary refuses to
emit a verdict.


\subsubsection{Reproducibility checklist (for reviewers)}\label{sec:3.5.4}

A reviewer wishing to
reproduce any number in \cref{sec:5} or \cref{sec:6.4} should perform the following.
We pin the anchor commit at \texttt{583b417} because it is the earliest
commit on \texttt{f2-methodology} at which every empirical CSV referenced
in the paper is committed (six files under \texttt{data/loop49/} plus 16
under \texttt{data/loop49\_swap/}); any descendant on the branch is also a
valid anchor.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \texttt{git checkout 583b417} (or any descendant of \texttt{f2-methodology}).
\item \texttt{cargo test --lib} exits 0 with 735 passing tests.
\item Pick any figure script in \texttt{papers/figures/}; run with no flags.
\item The script reads from the embedded \texttt{--input} default; verify the SHA of that input file against the value in the paper's appendix (\texttt{docs/F2\_RMS\_CDE.md} § Reproduce).
\item The generated PNG should be byte-equivalent (or visually identical modulo matplotlib version) to the figure in the paper.
\item The output JSONL should match the appendix's first-record signature.
\end{enumerate}

We claim \textbf{mechanical reproducibility} for \cref{sec:5} (figures regenerate from
public commits); we explicitly do \textbf{not} claim mechanical reproducibility
for the champion-scale follow-up of \texttt{docs/F2\_PRE\_REG.md}, which depends
on FineWeb data licensing and a specific hardware configuration.

\textbf{Implementation}: provenance preamble in \texttt{src/bin/f2\_ablation\_sweep.rs};
fingerprint mixin in \texttt{src/race/multi\_seed.rs} (\texttt{config\_fingerprint});
checker in \texttt{src/bin/f2\_provenance\_check.rs}; stratum banner in
\texttt{src/bin/f2\_dual\_mediation.rs} (\texttt{detect\_input\_stratum}) and
\texttt{src/bin/f2\_mediation\_sensitivity.rs} (\texttt{write\_stratum\_banner}).
The four disciplines above (\cref{sec:3.5.1}--\cref{sec:3.5.4}) are operationalized
through eight auxiliary scripts under \texttt{papers/scripts/} that a
reviewer can run to verify each invariant mechanically; the
complete catalogue and its required external tools are given in
Appendix E. The headline is a single-shot CI gate
(\texttt{papers/scripts/run\_all\_checks.sh}, ~60 s warm and 15--30 min
cold-clone) that chains every check plus \texttt{pack\_supplementary.sh},
exiting 0 only if all stages pass.



\section{Sandbox ablation matrix}\label{sec:4}



\subsection{Setup}\label{sec:4.1}


The empirical demonstration in \cref{sec:5} uses a deliberately small training
configuration: enough to surface the suppression structure cleanly, small
enough to fit a 5-seed $\times$ 80-cell sweep in ~25 minutes of wall time per
stratum on a single laptop. The full configuration is in Table 1.

\textbf{Table 1: sandbox configuration.}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
Parameter & Value \\
\midrule
Architecture & minimal transformer (1 attention layer + 1 FFN) \\
Parameters & ~8K (vocab=64, d\_model=128, d\_hidden=64) \\
Sequence length & 256 tokens \\
Training steps & 200 \\
Learning rate & 0.004 (linear warmup + constant) \\
Batch size & 1 (single sequence per step) \\
Seeds & {42, 43, 44, 45, 46} \\
Task & synthetic counter (running token count, deterministic) \\
Loss & cross-entropy with optional label smoothing \\
Default WD & 0.1 \\
Default warmup\_steps & 40 (= max(20, steps/5)) \\
Default dropout & 0.1 \\
Default label\_smoothing & 0.1 \\
Default grad\_clip & L2 norm at 1.0 \\
Default latent\_clamp & $\pm$1.0 on intermediate activations \\
RmsNorm & applied per BitLinear input \\
Quantization & Phi-ladder GFTernary$\to$GF8$\to$GF16$\to$GF32 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


\textbf{Seven canonical fixes ablated} (\texttt{race::ablation::CANONICAL\_FIX\_NAMES}):
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{rms} --- RmsNorm before each BitLinear
\item \texttt{warmup} --- linear LR warmup over \texttt{warmup\_steps} steps
\item \texttt{gradclip} --- L2 gradient norm clipped at 1.0
\item \texttt{clamp} --- latent activations clipped to $\pm$1.0
\item \texttt{smooth} --- label smoothing at $\varepsilon$ = 0.1
\item \texttt{wd} --- AdamW weight decay at $\lambda$ = 0.1
\item \texttt{dropout} --- applied to FFN output at p = 0.1
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Three strata} (\texttt{Stratum::ALL}):
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{Canonical} --- all defaults active
\item \texttt{Wd0} --- WD pinned to 0.0
\item \texttt{Warmup0} --- warmup\_steps pinned to 0
\end{itemize}

The ablation matrix per stratum contains:
\begin{itemize}
\item 8 cumulative-add rows (\texttt{baseline} through \texttt{full\_stack})
\item 7 LOCO rows (leave one fix out)
\item 21 pairwise rows (\texttt{pair\_<a>\_<b>} for every pair)
\item 35 triplet rows (\texttt{triplet\_<a>\_<b>\_<c>} for every triplet)
\item 1 \texttt{full\_stack} baseline (already counted)
\end{itemize}

This is 72 cells $\times$ 5 seeds = 360 training runs per stratum (rounding the
~80-cell figure above; the exact tally is \texttt{8 + 7 + 21 + 35 + 1}). With
three strata, \textbf{the full sandbox study comprises 1,080 training runs}.


\subsection{Why sandbox-scale}\label{sec:4.2}


The paper makes a methodological claim --- *stratified CDE analysis with
sensitivity envelopes is ready for routine use in ML training-recipe
ablation studies* --- and uses the sandbox study to \textbf{demonstrate} the
claim, not to \textbf{prove} it at scale. The demonstration only needs to be
detectable, reproducible, and analytically clean.

Three reasons we deliberately chose the small configuration:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Reproducibility on a laptop.} Anyone with a Rust toolchain can regenerate every number in \cref{sec:5} from the public commits in under one hour of wall time. This matches the reviewer reproducibility checklist in \cref{sec:3.5.4}. Champion-scale runs would require a GPU and FineWeb licensing, eliminating most reviewers.
\item \textbf{Mediation arithmetic is scale-invariant under the no-interaction assumption.} The Daniel et al. identification result depends on the conditional expectations being linear in the mediator and exposure structure; if it holds at sandbox scale, the same decomposition formulas apply at champion scale (only the numerical magnitudes change). The \texttt{dual\_mediation\_no\_interaction\_residual\_lock} test confirms the linearity assumption holds in our regime to within $10^{-6}$.
\item \textbf{Sign-flip demonstration value.} The headline finding (RmsNorm NDE flips sign across strata) is qualitative, not quantitative. A reviewer who sees the canonical $-$4.12 BPB versus the wd0 +0.43 BPB result --- even on a synthetic task --- cannot dismiss the qualitative point with "your task is too small." Magnitude estimates obviously do not transfer; the \emph{existence of a stratum-induced sign flip} does.
\end{enumerate}

The champion-scale validation is pre-registered in \texttt{docs/F2\_PRE\_REG.md}
and is contingent on a future compute decision (see \cref{sec:10.2}).



\section{Empirical results}\label{sec:5}


All results in this section come from the sandbox ablation matrix (\cref{sec:4}):
five non-mediator fixes (rms, dropout, gradclip, clamp, smooth), five
seeds (42--46), 200 training steps per cell, ~8K parameters, synthetic
counter task. Mediator pair fixed at \texttt{M\_1 = wd}, \texttt{M\_2 = warmup} unless
noted. Confidence intervals are 95\% Student-t at df = N$-$1 = 4 per \cref{sec:3.2}.


\subsection{Canonical ablation --- the suppression pattern}\label{sec:5.1}


Under canonical mediation (no stratum constraint), the dual\_mediation
decomposition reveals a striking pattern: every non-mediator fix has a
large positive indirect effect via WD canceled by a comparably large
negative direct effect.

Table 1 (Figure 3) shows the 5$\times$4 PSE matrix:

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lllll}
\toprule
 & NDE & NIE\_M1 & NIE\_M2 & NIE\_chain \\
\midrule
rms & $-$4.12 & +4.99 & +1.27 & $-$1.27 \\
dropout & $-$4.55 & +4.46 & +0.06 & $-$0.05 \\
gradclip & $-$4.74 & +4.73 & +0.11 & $-$0.11 \\
clamp & $-$4.87 & +4.87 & +0.32 & $-$0.33 \\
smooth & $-$4.87 & +4.87 & +0.32 & $-$0.33 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


(BPB units; per-row sum recovers \texttt{Δ\_X} to within $10^{-6}$.)

The NIE\_M1 column (effect mediated through WD) is uniformly $\approx$+5 BPB; the
NDE column is uniformly $\approx$$-$5 BPB. \textbf{The net total effect \texttt{Δ\_X} is small for every fix except rms (\texttt{+0.87 BPB})} because the WD pathway absorbs
the apparent harm of removing each fix.

A naive seed-mean analysis on the canonical CSV would report each fix's
total effect as "approximately zero with overlapping CIs" and conclude
that the methodology stack has no effect --- a conclusion that misses the
suppression structure entirely.

\textbf{Figure 3}: 5$\times$4 PSE heatmap. Bold-bordered cells have CIs that exclude
zero; visually, the red NDE column and the green NIE\_M1 column are both
universally bold, reflecting the systematic suppression.


\subsection{wd0 stratum (Pearl CDE on WD) --- the sign flip}\label{sec:5.2}


When we stratify on WD = 0 (Pearl CDE with WD's pathway structurally
blocked), the NIE\_M1 column trivially zeros out (the mediator is pinned).
The interesting column is now the NDE --- the \emph{direct} effect with WD
held constant.

Table 2 compares per-fix NDE across the three strata (canonical,
wd0, warmup0):

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lllll}
\toprule
fix & NDE\_canonical (95\% CI) & NDE\_wd0 (95\% CI) & NDE\_warmup0 (95\% CI) & rms-style sign flip? \\
\midrule
\textbf{rms} & \textbf{$-$4.12 [$-$4.68, $-$3.55]} & \textbf{+0.43 [+0.01, +0.84]} & \textbf{$-$4.12 [$-$4.70, $-$3.55]} & \textbf{yes} \\
dropout & $-$4.55 [$-$4.89, $-$4.22] & $-$0.01 [$-$0.34, +0.33] & $-$4.56 [$-$4.90, $-$4.21] & no (CI brackets 0) \\
gradclip & $-$4.74 [$-$5.00, $-$4.49] & $-$0.20 [$-$0.67, +0.27] & $-$4.75 [$-$4.98, $-$4.52] & no (CI brackets 0) \\
clamp & $-$4.87 [$-$4.88, $-$4.86] & $-$0.32 [$-$0.61, $-$0.04] & $-$4.87 [$-$4.91, $-$4.84] & no (magnitude ~15$\times$ smaller) \\
smooth & $-$4.87 [$-$4.88, $-$4.86] & $-$0.32 [$-$0.61, $-$0.04] & $-$4.87 [$-$4.91, $-$4.84] & no (magnitude ~15$\times$ smaller) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


The wd0 stratum has two stories. \textbf{Only RmsNorm crosses zero}: the
canonical "removing rms helps BPB by 4.12" estimate is, under Pearl
CDE at WD=0, "removing rms hurts BPB by 0.43" --- and the 95\% CI
excludes zero by only 0.01 BPB (\texttt{Γ\_tip(Λ=1.0) = 1.01} per \cref{sec:5.4},
\textbf{fragile} per the \cref{sec:3.3} reporting convention --- the wd0 finding's
sign is well-determined but its robustness to unmeasured confounding
is essentially the same as the CI margin itself). But \textbf{all four non-rms fixes also collapse in magnitude} at wd0 --- the canonical ~$-$4.5 to $-$4.9
BPB direct effect drops to between $-$0.01 and $-$0.32 BPB. Two of the
four (dropout, gradclip) have 95\% CIs that now bracket zero; the
other two (clamp, smooth) have small but distinguishable negative
effects. The wd0 stratum is therefore a structural attenuator on
the entire NDE column, not just a sign-flipper for RmsNorm; what
distinguishes RmsNorm is that the attenuation overshoots into
positive territory.

The warmup0 stratum, by contrast, reproduces the canonical NDE
column almost line-by-line --- every fix's warmup0 estimate is within
0.05 BPB of its canonical estimate. This rules out "any non-default
stratum flips the sign" as an explanation; the wd0 finding is
specifically tied to weight decay's structural role, not to
stratification \emph{per se}.

\textbf{Why wd=0 is a meaningful counterfactual, not a pathological state.}
A reviewer may ask whether the wd0 stratum is degenerate --- perhaps
the model in this regime is not in a useful operating point and the
canonical NDE is "the real answer". Three observations push back:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Published recipes operate at WD $\approx$ 0.} The pre-AdamW transformer literature (Vaswani et al. 2017, \emph{Attention is All You Need}; many 2017--2018 fairseq defaults) treated WD as an optional knob and shipped with WD $\in$ {0, 0.01}. Decoupled-WD (Loshchilov \& Hutter 2019, "Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization", ICLR; originally \citep{arxiv:1711.05101} in 2017) explicitly argues that prior practice under-used WD because of the Adam-coupling pitfall. Low-precision-training ablation work routinely holds WD at zero or very low values to isolate quantization effects from regularization effects. Pinning WD=0 therefore reproduces a real published configuration, not a degenerate one.
\item \textbf{The trainer remains stable at WD=0} in our sandbox: every wd0 seed produces a finite, non-NaN final BPB, and per-seed BPB CVs are within the \cref{sec:3.5.4} stability tolerance. There is no divergence-based reason to dismiss the stratum.
\item \textbf{The framework is symmetric in its strata-choice machinery.} The warmup0 stratum produces the \emph{same direction} of NDE as the canonical stratum ($-$4.12 vs $-$4.12 --- see Table 2), so the sign-flip is specifically tied to WD-pinning, not to "any non-default stratum". This is the asymmetry the framework is designed to surface; it would not appear if wd0 were merely a degenerate state.
\end{enumerate}

This is the headline finding of the paper. \textbf{Figure 4} visualizes the
three NDE values for rms (canonical, wd0, warmup0) with error bars.
We frame this finding as a *unit-test demonstration on a synthetic
task* that the framework can detect a sign flip when one is
constructed --- not as a final ML finding about RmsNorm's intrinsic
behavior at champion scale. See \cref{sec:1.2} and \cref{sec:10.1} for venue calibration.


\subsection{Cross-stratum stability flag}\label{sec:5.3}


\textbf{Caveat upfront.} The \texttt{f2\_stratum\_compare} comparator is a
mechanical bookkeeping device, not a substantive empirical finding
in itself. Its 20-row output for the M\_1=wd, M\_2=warmup
parameterization fires \texttt{stable\_across\_strata = true} for 4 rows
and \texttt{false} for 16 rows, but on inspection \textbf{both verdicts are explained by structural artifacts}, not by substantive cross-
stratum comparison. The interesting result of \cref{sec:5} is the swap row
discussed under \cref{sec:5.3}'s "Swap parameterization" subhead below;
the bare 16/4 split should not be read as a finding.

\texttt{f2\_stratum\_compare} joins per-fix PSEs across the three strata and
flags each row with \texttt{stable\_across\_strata = true} iff every pair of
present 95\% CIs has non-empty intersection. The committed output at
\texttt{data/loop49/loop49\_3stratum.csv} (M\_1=wd, M\_2=warmup parameterization,
20 rows = 5 fixes $\times$ 4 PSEs) shows:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{16 PSEs flagged \texttt{false}}. These are dominated by rows where the M\_1=wd PSE column (NIE\_M1) is trivially zero in the wd0 stratum because the mediator is pinned --- by construction, the wd-mediated indirect effect at wd=0 is exactly zero. The stability flag correctly fires on this \emph{structural} disagreement; the flag is faithfully reporting that an apples-to-apples comparison is not possible when the mediator is pinned. This is a tautology of the Pearl CDE definition, not an empirical finding.
\item \textbf{4 PSEs flagged \texttt{true}} (gradclip and dropout NIE\_M2 and NIE\_chain). These are the small-effect rows whose CIs all bracket zero in every stratum, so the overlap test trivially succeeds --- another structural artifact (this time of small-effect-with-wide-CI rows), not a substantive cross-stratum invariance.
\end{itemize}

What this empirically demonstrates is the comparator's \emph{plumbing},
not a substantive finding: the comparator surfaces stratum-induced
disagreement loudly, and the analyst reads the flag with knowledge
of why each disagreement exists. The substantive cross-stratum
result emerges from the swap parameterization below, where one row
(\texttt{wd x NIE\_M1} via rms) survives identical across all three strata
for non-trivial reasons.

\textbf{Swap parameterization --- Phase 0 result (Loop 64).} A natural
follow-up analysis re-runs the four-PSE decomposition with
\texttt{(M\_1 = rms, M\_2 = warmup)} instead, to obtain an NIE\_M1 estimate
that quantifies "the part of X's effect mediated by rms" for each
non-mediator X. Pre-registered in section 4.5 of \texttt{docs/F2\_PRE\_REG.md} and executed
in Loop 64 against the regenerated \texttt{--mode all} canonical sweep
plus the two committed stratified sweeps; outputs are committed at
\texttt{data/loop49\_swap/}. Of the 20 rows in
\texttt{data/loop49\_swap/3stratum\_swap.csv}, \textbf{5 are flagged \texttt{stable\_across\_strata = true}} under CI-overlap. The
substantively interesting row is:

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
stratum & X = wd, NIE\_M1 via rms (95\% CI) \\
\midrule
canonical & \textbf{$-$0.751 [$-$1.325, $-$0.177]} \\
wd0 & $-$0.751 [$-$1.325, $-$0.177] (identical) \\
warmup0 & $-$0.751 [$-$1.325, $-$0.177] (identical) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


The byte-identical values are not an overclaim but an artifact of
the no-XM-interaction structure plus the deterministic per-seed
LOCO/pair/triplet sweep design: under the swap parameterization
the NIE\_M1 closed form reduces to \texttt{Δ\_\{X, M\_2\} − Δ\_\{X, M\_1, M\_2\}},
which evaluates from the same pair/triplet sweep rows regardless
of the stratum's baseline-config choice when the mediator-pinning
does not interact with the rms-mediated pathway. The
\texttt{dual\_mediation\_no\_interaction\_residual\_lock} test (\cref{sec:8.2}) validates
the residual at $< 10^{-6}$ for the canonical parameterization;
Phase 0 confirms the equivalence empirically holds under swap.
We interpret this row narrowly as evidence that \textbf{the rms-mediated NIE-via-WD for the wd fix specifically is the only PSE whose value survives identical across all three stratum reference points} --- a real result, but a much narrower claim than an
"all PSEs invariant" assertion.

\textbf{Figure 5} visualizes the swap-parameterization NIE\_M1 matrix
across the three strata. The byte-identical wd row at the bottom
is the only fully-invariant row; the other four fixes show
variation in the wd0 column (the WD-pinned stratum) while
canonical and warmup0 columns match each other --- a structural
pattern consistent with the wd0 stratum being the only one that
constrains the wd path.

\textbf{Robustness to the M\_2 choice.} A reviewer may ask whether the
byte-identical pattern depends on the specific M\_2 = warmup choice
in the swap parameterization. \cref{sec:6.4} reports the full M\_2 sensitivity
sweep across all five candidate mediators. The headline result
moved there: the invariance is \textbf{conditional on M\_2 matching the warmup0 stratum's pinned variable}; under the four alternative M\_2
choices, the weaker canonical = wd0 invariance still holds in
every case (a structural consequence of wd being target X, not a
mediator on the rms-M\_2 path), but the full triple-stratum
invariance does not.


\subsection{Sensitivity envelope}\label{sec:5.4}


\textbf{On the choice of $\Lambda$.} \cref{sec:3.3} introduces $\Lambda$ as a free parameter of
the bridge-score envelope (it specifies the maximum BPB shift an
unmeasured confounder could induce on the outcome residual). We
report headline estimates at \textbf{$\Lambda$ = 1.0 BPB} because that is the
unit-scale of the BPB axis itself: an unmeasured confounder whose
outcome-residual envelope is 1.0 BPB represents a confounder
comparable in magnitude to a \emph{full bit per byte} of explanatory
power --- i.e., on the scale of the empirical effects in \cref{sec:5.1}---\cref{sec:5.3}.
Smaller $\Lambda$ (e.g., 0.1) treats only sub-decibit confounders; larger
$\Lambda$ (e.g., 5.0) treats confounders larger than the entire effect of
typical ablations. The $\Lambda$ = 1.0 baseline is a calibration choice,
not a derived quantity; we show the full $\Lambda$ $\in$ [0.1, 5.0] sweep in
Figure 2 so a reviewer can re-classify at any $\Lambda$ they prefer.

Per \cref{sec:3.3}, we report tipping-point \texttt{Γ\_tip(Λ=1.0)} and the
VanderWeele-Ding classification for each headline estimate:

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Estimate & $\Gamma$\_tip($\Lambda$=1.0) & Class \\
\midrule
Canonical NDE for rms ($-$4.12) & 4.55 & robust \\
Canonical NIE\_M1 via WD (+4.99) & 5.42 & robust \\
wd0 CDE for rms (+0.43) & 1.01 & fragile \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


\textbf{Full canonical-stratum envelope (all 20 PSEs).} The headline
table above gives the three highest-relevance estimates; we
classify every PSE in the canonical stratum against the same
envelope at $\Lambda$ = 1.0, grouped by classification tier:

\textbf{Robust} ($\Gamma$\_tip $\geq$ 2.0) --- the 10 NDE + NIE\_M1 rows survive
substantial unmeasured confounding:

\begin{itemize}
\item rms NDE: $-$4.12 [$-$4.68, $-$3.55], $\Gamma$\_tip = 4.55
\item rms NIE\_M1: +4.99 [+4.42, +5.56], $\Gamma$\_tip = 5.42
\item dropout NDE: $-$4.55 [$-$4.89, $-$4.22], $\Gamma$\_tip = 5.22
\item dropout NIE\_M1: +4.46 [+4.10, +4.82], $\Gamma$\_tip = 5.10
\item gradclip NDE: $-$4.74 [$-$5.00, $-$4.49], $\Gamma$\_tip = 5.49
\item gradclip NIE\_M1: +4.73 [+4.48, +4.99], $\Gamma$\_tip = 5.48
\item clamp NDE: $-$4.87 [$-$4.88, $-$4.86], $\Gamma$\_tip = 5.86
\item clamp NIE\_M1: +4.87 [+4.84, +4.91], $\Gamma$\_tip = 5.84
\item smooth NDE: $-$4.87 [$-$4.88, $-$4.86], $\Gamma$\_tip = 5.86
\item smooth NIE\_M1: +4.87 [+4.84, +4.91], $\Gamma$\_tip = 5.84
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Moderate} (1.25 $\leq$ $\Gamma$\_tip < 2.0):

\begin{itemize}
\item rms NIE\_M2: +1.27 [+0.51, +2.02], $\Gamma$\_tip = 1.51
\item rms NIE\_chain: $-$1.27 [$-$2.02, $-$0.51], $\Gamma$\_tip = 1.51
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Fragile} ($\Gamma$\_tip < 1.25):

\begin{itemize}
\item dropout NIE\_M2: +0.06 [$-$0.43, +0.54] (CI brackets 0), $\Gamma$\_tip = 1.00
\item dropout NIE\_chain: $-$0.05 [$-$0.56, +0.46] (CI brackets 0), $\Gamma$\_tip = 1.00
\item gradclip NIE\_M2: +0.11 [$-$0.34, +0.56] (CI brackets 0), $\Gamma$\_tip = 1.00
\item gradclip NIE\_chain: $-$0.11 [$-$0.55, +0.34] (CI brackets 0), $\Gamma$\_tip = 1.00
\item clamp NIE\_M2: +0.32 [+0.04, +0.61], $\Gamma$\_tip = 1.04
\item clamp NIE\_chain: $-$0.33 [$-$0.62, $-$0.04], $\Gamma$\_tip = 1.04
\item smooth NIE\_M2: +0.32 [+0.04, +0.61], $\Gamma$\_tip = 1.04
\item smooth NIE\_chain: $-$0.33 [$-$0.62, $-$0.04], $\Gamma$\_tip = 1.04
\end{itemize}

The headline pattern: \textbf{the NDE and NIE\_M1 rows are uniformly robust} ($\Gamma$\_tip > 5 for every fix), reinforcing the \cref{sec:5.2} reading
that the suppression structure is uniform across the ablation
column. The \textbf{NIE\_M2 and NIE\_chain rows are uniformly fragile}
($\Gamma$\_tip near 1.0), which is the bridge-score envelope confirming
what the \cref{sec:5.3} cross-stratum comparator surfaced as small-effect
bracketing-zero artifacts. The full canonical envelope thus
sharpens the \cref{sec:5.3} reading: the small-effect rows are not just
small under naive CI inspection, they are also fragile under
unmeasured-confounding stress at $\Lambda$ = 1.0.

\textbf{Figure 2} plots the full \texttt{Γ\_tip(Λ)} hyperbolae for rms's four PSEs
over \texttt{Λ in [0.1, 5.0]} BPB. The crossover at \texttt{Λ \~\{\} 1.5} is where the
NIE\_M2 and NIE\_chain estimates leave the moderate range and become
fragile.

The honest reading: the \textbf{canonical NIE\_M1} ("WD as mediator") result
is robust under E-value-style stress testing --- $\Gamma$\_tip > 5 means any
unmeasured confounder would have to be substantially stronger than
typical training-recipe correlates to overturn the verdict. The
\textbf{wd0 NDE} ("rms-intrinsic-effect-under-WD-pinning") result is the
more fragile claim, with $\Gamma$\_tip = 1.01 placing it firmly in the
\textbf{fragile} tier: the bridge-score envelope reaches zero almost
immediately, reflecting the empirical reality that the 95\% CI on
this estimate excludes zero by only 0.01 BPB. The sign-flip
\emph{across} strata is the qualitatively interesting finding; the wd0
magnitude itself should be read as "sign well-determined,
magnitude fragile under any unmeasured-confounder stress test of
the bridge-score envelope at $\Lambda$ $\geq$ 0.01 BPB".

\textbf{On the prior 1.43 reported in earlier drafts.} Drafts prior to
An earlier draft reported the wd0 row as \texttt{Γ\_tip = 1.43}, computed using
the \emph{point estimate} (+0.43) instead of the \emph{closer CI endpoint}
(+0.01) in the \cref{sec:3.3} envelope inversion. The \cref{sec:3.3} formula
\texttt{Γ\_tip(Λ) = 1 + min(|CI\_lo|, |CI\_hi|) / Λ} mandates the CI
endpoint, not the point estimate; the correct value at $\Lambda$ = 1.0
is \texttt{1 + 0.01 / 1.0 = 1.01}. The prior 1.43 was discovered by the
25th adversarial pass and corrected in the same loop.
The implementation in \texttt{src/bin/f2\_mediation\_sensitivity.rs:236}
has always used the CI-endpoint convention; the discrepancy was
in the manuscript table, not the code.



\section{Sensitivity to choices}\label{sec:6}


The headline finding in \cref{sec:5} depends on three modelling choices that a
reviewer would reasonably interrogate: which mediator pair \texttt{(M\_1, M\_2)}
we decompose against, which statistical family we use for confidence
intervals, and which strata we run. We address each in turn.


\subsection{Mediator pair (M\_1, M\_2)}\label{sec:6.1}


The default decomposition uses \texttt{M\_1 = wd, M\_2 = warmup}, motivated by
prior mediation analyses in this framework that identified WD and
warmup as the two strongest mediators in the canonical
ablation matrix. A reviewer might object that the chosen pair determines
the sign of NIE\_M2 by construction.

To address this, the swap parameterization \texttt{M\_1 = rms, M\_2 = warmup}
is the natural replication: RmsNorm itself becomes the candidate
mediator, and the question becomes "what fraction of each
non-mediator fix's effect runs through RmsNorm?" Under no-XM-
interaction, the framework predicts that the rms-mediated NIE
should be approximately stable across the wd0 stratum, since
pinning wd does not directly constrain the rms-mediated pathway.
The three-stratum swap-parameterization run is committed at
\texttt{data/loop49\_swap/} (Phase 0 deliverable, completed Loop 64); see
\cref{sec:5.3} for the wd $\times$ NIE\_M1 byte-identical result and \cref{sec:6.4} for the
full M\_2 robustness landscape. The swap parameterization is
therefore not a hypothetical sensitivity check but an
empirically-anchored result reported in this paper.


\subsection{Statistic family}\label{sec:6.2}


We use \textbf{paired Student-t} confidence intervals at \texttt{df = N − 1 = 4} for
all point estimates in \cref{sec:5}. Two alternative families exist and were
considered:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Exact permutation tests} (\texttt{f2\_iloco\_score --permutation}). At \texttt{N = 5}, the sign-flip null distribution of the 32 paired-sign permutations gives \texttt{2/32 = 0.0625} as the minimum two-sided p-value. This is exact under exchangeability but provides only one significant digit of resolution. We use permutation tests for the iLOCO module but not for the dual-mediation PSEs because the resolution is too coarse for tipping-point analysis.
\item \textbf{BCa bootstrap}. Bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap at N=5 is well known to under-cover empirically (the motivating evidence in the Owen 2025 reference we cited in \cref{sec:3.2}). We do not use BCa for any reported result.
\item \textbf{Bootstrap-t / Beta-weighted bootstrap-t}. The Owen (2025) Beta- weighted bootstrap-t (\citep{arxiv:2508.10083}) is the strongest small-N alternative we are aware of, but it requires simulation calibration per estimand. At our sandbox scale we judged the additional complexity unjustified; for the champion-scale follow-up in \texttt{docs/F2\_PRE\_REG.md} we plan to add it as an alternative CI.
\end{itemize}

The Student-t choice is conservative-leaning at small N: it widens the
CI relative to a Gaussian approximation, which makes the wd0 NDE result
(\texttt{+0.43 [+0.01, +0.84]}) harder to obtain. A skeptical reviewer should
read "this CI excludes zero under Student-t" as a stronger claim than
the same conclusion under Gaussian.


\subsection{Strata}\label{sec:6.3}


We chose \texttt{Wd0} and \texttt{Warmup0} based on prior mediation analyses
(\texttt{docs/F2\_RMS\_CDE.md}) that identified WD and warmup as the
two strongest mediators in the canonical ablation matrix. Three other
candidate strata are pre-defined in the framework but not run for this
paper:

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{LabelSmoothing0} (label smoothing pinned to $\varepsilon$ = 0.0)
\item \texttt{ClampZero} (latent clamp disabled)
\item \texttt{Dropout0} (dropout pinned to p = 0.0)
\end{itemize}

The selection criteria for adding a new stratum are documented in the
\texttt{Stratum} enum doc comment in \texttt{src/race/ablation.rs}: a variant is added
when the corresponding fix exhibits $\geq$ 50\% indirect-effect share in a
canonical mediation analysis, and when the Pearl CDE at the disabled
value is the natural next analytical question. None of the three skipped
strata met both criteria in our preliminary analyses; we leave them as
future work.

A meta-objection a reviewer might raise: "you chose to stratify on the
mediators that produce the cleanest sign-flip story." We do not
deny that incentive exists; we cite the cross-stratum invariant in \cref{sec:5.3}
(invariant under both parameterizations) as the structural result that
is independent of which particular mediator pair was chosen.


\subsection{M\_2 robustness --- full sweep}\label{sec:6.4}


\cref{sec:5.3} reports that the swap-parameterization NIE\_M1 via rms for
X = wd is byte-identical across all three strata under
(M\_1 = rms, M\_2 = warmup). A natural follow-up is whether the
invariance depends on M\_2 = warmup specifically. We re-ran the
swap analysis with \texttt{(M\_1 = rms, M\_2 = m)} for every non-mediator
candidate \texttt{m in \{gradclip, clamp, smooth, dropout\}} across all
three strata; outputs committed at
\texttt{data/loop49\_swap/\{canonical,wd0,warmup0\}\_swap\_m2\{m\}.csv} (12
new CSVs). Result for \texttt{X = wd, NIE\_M1} via rms:

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lllll}
\toprule
M\_2 = \dots{} & canonical & wd0 & warmup0 & All 3 identical? \\
\midrule
\textbf{warmup} & \textbf{$-$0.751 [$-$1.325, $-$0.177]} & \textbf{$-$0.751 [$-$1.325, $-$0.177]} & \textbf{$-$0.751 [$-$1.325, $-$0.177]} & \textbf{YES} \\
gradclip & $-$1.781 [$-$2.210, $-$1.353] & $-$1.781 [$-$2.210, $-$1.353] & $-$0.626 [$-$1.341, +0.090] & No (warmup0) \\
clamp & $-$1.693 [$-$2.162, $-$1.225] & $-$1.693 [$-$2.162, $-$1.225] & $-$0.751 [$-$1.325, $-$0.177] & No (warmup0) \\
smooth & $-$1.693 [$-$2.162, $-$1.225] & $-$1.693 [$-$2.162, $-$1.225] & $-$0.751 [$-$1.325, $-$0.177] & No (warmup0) \\
dropout & $-$1.625 [$-$1.819, $-$1.431] & $-$1.625 [$-$1.819, $-$1.431] & $-$0.400 [$-$0.787, $-$0.014] & No (warmup0) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


The pattern across all five M\_2 alternatives is exactly what
no-XM-interaction predicts:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{wd0 = canonical in every row.} The wd0 stratum pins a variable (\texttt{weight\_decay}) that is the \emph{outcome target} X for this row, not a mediator on the rms-M\_2 path. Removing wd does not constrain the rms-mediated indirect effect, so the per-seed \texttt{pair\_X\_M\_2} and \texttt{triplet\_X\_M\_1\_M\_2} rows used in the NIE\_M1 closed form are byte-identical in canonical and wd0 sweeps.
\item \textbf{warmup0 diverges from canonical/wd0 unless M\_2 = warmup.} The warmup0 stratum pins warmup. If the swap parameterization already has M\_2 = warmup, the stratum pinning and the parameterization align: the M\_2 path is the stratum-fixed path, and the formula gives the same result everywhere. For any other M\_2 choice, warmup is \emph{also} a covariate that takes its sweep value in canonical/wd0 but is pinned to 0 in warmup0 --- so the per-seed BPB shifts and the NIE\_M1 estimate diverges.
\end{enumerate}

The narrow scoping is therefore: \textbf{the wd $\times$ NIE\_M1 via rms row is byte-identical across all three strata only when the swap parameterization's M\_2 is precisely the variable pinned by the warmup0 stratum.} Under the four alternative M\_2 choices, the
weaker invariance (canonical = wd0) holds in 4 of 4 cases, but
the full-triple-stratum invariance does not. \textbf{Figure 6}
visualizes the full 5 $\times$ 3 landscape with thick row outline
marking the warmup row's full invariance.



\section{Limitations}\label{sec:7}


We list six limitations the paper's claims are subject to,
grouped into four clusters: scope/external validity, statistical
power, identification assumptions, and framework scope. Each is
acknowledged here so a future reader can verify the framework is
being applied within its valid scope.


\subsection{Scope and external validity}\label{sec:7.1}


\textbf{Sandbox-scale only.} The 200-step, ~8K-parameter, single-batch
   configuration of \cref{sec:4} is a stress test for the methodology, not a
   champion-scale claim. The headline result (RmsNorm CDE sign flip)
   surfaces a \emph{qualitative} phenomenon (suppression by WD) that we
   expect to generalize to larger scales, but the specific magnitudes
   ($-$4.12 vs +0.43) do not transfer. Champion-scale validation is
   pre-registered in \texttt{docs/F2\_PRE\_REG.md}.


\subsection{Statistical power}\label{sec:7.2}


\textbf{Five seeds is small.} Owen (2025, \citep{arxiv:2508.10083}) and a related
   literature on N$\leq$5 inference (see \cref{sec:3.2}) argue that Student-t intervals
   at df=4 are the most defensible default in this regime. We adopt this
   choice deliberately, but report all numerical results in \cref{sec:5} with the
   understanding that the minimum-detectable effect at N=5 is bounded
   below by $t_{0.975, 4} \cdot \mathrm{SE} \approx 2.776 \cdot \mathrm{SE}$. For the wd0 CDE of +0.43
   BPB with SE $\approx$ 0.15, the lower CI endpoint is +0.01 BPB; the result
   excludes zero by 0.01 BPB, a 7\% margin. A larger seed budget would
   yield tighter CIs and might or might not preserve the sign-flip
   verdict.


\subsection{Identification assumptions}\label{sec:7.3}


\textbf{No exposure-mediator interaction is assumed.} The Daniel et al.
   identification result (\cref{sec:3.2}) requires both sequential ignorability
   and a no-interaction assumption between the exposure \texttt{X} and the
   mediators \texttt{(M\_1, M\_2)}. The latter is testable: we report empirically
   that the residual
   \texttt{Δ\_X − (NDE + NIE\_M1 + NIE\_M2 + NIE\_chain)} is below $10^{-6}$ in our
   regime, validated by the
   \texttt{dual\_mediation\_no\_interaction\_residual\_lock} test (Loop 34). We do
   not test sequential ignorability directly; the bridge-score envelope
   (\cref{sec:3.3}) is our defense against unmeasured confounding.

\textbf{Synthetic counter task is not a language model.} The training task
   we use is a deterministic counter: the target at each step is a
   simple function of the running token count. This is an
   analytical-tractability choice that gives a clean signal at small
   scale. The pattern of WD suppression and RmsNorm sign-flip could in
   principle be specific to this task. The pre-registered FineWeb
   validation in \texttt{docs/F2\_PRE\_REG.md} is the appropriate next step.


\subsection{Framework scope}\label{sec:7.4}


\textbf{The framework supports two-mediator decomposition only.} Adding a
   third mediator requires reworking the identification arithmetic; we
   have not done so. We currently work around this by re-running the
   analysis with different \texttt{(M\_1, M\_2)} choices (the Loop 50 swap in
   \cref{sec:6.1} is one example) and looking for cross-pairing invariance as
   evidence of structural effects. A formal three-mediator extension
   is left as future work.

\textbf{No post-treatment / intermediate confounders.} The Daniel et al.
   identification (\cref{sec:3.2}) assumes that any confounder of the mediators
   \texttt{(M\_1, M\_2)} is \emph{pre-treatment} --- measured before the intervention
   \texttt{X} is applied. If a mediator is itself caused by \texttt{X} and also
   confounds the second mediator (a \emph{treatment-induced confounder},
   per Rudolph \& Díaz 2023, \citep{arxiv:2205.04408}), the standard Daniel et al.
   identification fails and the four-PSE decomposition is not
   point-identifiable. In our setting \texttt{X} is a discrete intervention
   on training-recipe knobs and the candidate mediators
   \texttt{(wd, warmup, gradclip, clamp, smooth, dropout)} are all \emph{also}
   training-recipe knobs that are set at the same configuration step
   as \texttt{X}. We argue this regime is closer to pre-treatment than to
   post-treatment because the configuration choice for one knob is
   not causally downstream of the choice for another --- the analyst
   sets them jointly, not sequentially. A reviewer who disagrees with
   this framing should consult Hong, Yang \& Qin (2023,
   \citep{arxiv:2107.11014}) for the post-treatment sensitivity analysis they
   would impose instead, or Díaz et al. (2021, \citep{arxiv:1912.09936}) for
   the interventional-effects framework that point-identifies a
   related estimand without the no-post-treatment assumption. We
   leave a formal post-treatment extension of F2 as future work.



\section{Software}\label{sec:8}


The F2 framework is implemented as a Rust 1.82 crate, MIT-licensed and
single-process. The codebase is anchored at commit \texttt{583b417} for every
empirical result in \cref{sec:5}; the test inventory in Appendix D is
auto-generated from that anchor commit.


\subsection{Binaries}\label{sec:8.1}


Ten F2 binaries form a Unix-style pipeline over the long-form CSV
contract documented in \cref{sec:3.5.2}. Each binary reads zero or more CSVs,
emits one CSV, and validates W3C-PROV preambles on entry. The full
index, including per-binary CLI synopses, lives in \texttt{docs/F2\_BINARIES.md};
the binaries cited in \cref{sec:5} are:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{\texttt{f2\_ablation\_sweep}} --- run a single ablation sweep at one stratum; write a long-form CSV with ModeKind $\times$ Stratum tagged rows.
\item \textbf{\texttt{f2\_dual\_mediation}} --- apply the Daniel et al. 4-PSE decomposition (\cref{sec:3.2}) to a sweep CSV; emit per-PSE estimates + \texttt{t}-CIs.
\item \textbf{\texttt{f2\_mediation\_sensitivity}} --- compute the bridge-score envelope (\cref{sec:3.3}) with \texttt{--lambda-grid} / \texttt{--tipping-point} / \texttt{--wide-form} modes.
\item \textbf{\texttt{f2\_stratum\_compare}} --- take the canonical, wd0, and warmup0 CSVs; emit the cross-stratum comparison with \texttt{stable\_across\_strata} flags (\cref{sec:3.4}).
\item \textbf{\texttt{f2\_to\_jsonl}} --- stream-convert a CSV to JSON Lines for matplotlib and downstream tooling.
\item \textbf{\texttt{f2\_provenance\_check}} --- validate that a CSV's W3C-PROV preamble matches the current \texttt{TRAINER\_INTERNALS\_SCHEMA}; exit codes drive CI.
\end{itemize}

The remaining four binaries (\texttt{f2\_ablation\_aggregate}, \texttt{f2\_iloco\_dot},
\texttt{f2\_iloco\_score}, \texttt{f2\_mediation}) cover aggregation, ILOCO scoring,
and the single-mediator legacy path; they are documented for
completeness in the binaries index.


\subsection{Tests}\label{sec:8.2}


The auto-generated Appendix D inventory (regenerable via
\texttt{papers/scripts/generate\_appendix\_d.sh}) lists 830 tests grouped by
source: 735 in \texttt{src/lib.rs}, the remainder distributed across
per-binary unit tests and seven integration suites under \texttt{tests/}. Two
regression locks deserve a direct mention because they back load-
bearing claims in \cref{sec:3}:

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{dual\_mediation\_no\_interaction\_residual\_lock} --- locks the Daniel et al. residual closure under our no-interaction assumption against the four-path estimator; if the residual term \texttt{Δ\_X − (NDE + NIE\_\{M\_1\} + NIE\_\{M\_2\} + NIE\_chain)} ever exceeds a fixed tolerance ($1 \times 10^{-6}$), the test fails and forces a retraction of the delta-method SE formula. The lock certifies algebraic equivalence to the Daniel et al. decomposition only; the Miles-Shpitser single-pathway EIF (\cref{sec:2.1}) is invoked as motivational, not as a target the lock verifies against.
\item \texttt{trainer\_internals\_schema\_is\_load\_bearing} --- locks the \texttt{TRAINER\_INTERNALS\_SCHEMA} constant into the config-fingerprint hash, so any internal schema bump produces a deterministic fingerprint change. This is the mechanism that makes the reproducibility checklist in \cref{sec:3.5.4} surface schema drift as a hard \texttt{f2\_provenance\_check} failure rather than as a silent BPB shift.
\end{itemize}


\subsection{Provenance and empirical data}\label{sec:8.3}


Every CSV emitted by F2 binaries opens with a W3C-PROV preamble:
\texttt{\# prov:generatedBy}, \texttt{\# prov:wasDerivedFrom}, \texttt{\# prov:atTime},
\texttt{\# git\_sha}, \texttt{\# config\_fingerprint}. The preamble is validated on
entry to every downstream binary; the validation rules and exit codes
are specified in \cref{sec:3.5.1} and locked by the
\texttt{f2\_provenance\_check\_exit\_codes} integration suite.

The six CSVs that back the headline finding in \cref{sec:5} are anchored at
\texttt{data/loop49/} with MD5 checksums and per-file reproduction commands
in the directory's \texttt{README.md}. Reproducing \cref{sec:5} byte-for-byte requires
nothing beyond a \texttt{git checkout} of the anchor commit and the commands
listed in \cref{sec:3.5.4}.



\section{Related work}\label{sec:9}


We situate F2 against three adjacent literatures: ML ablation
methodology, causal mediation theory, and sensitivity analysis. We also
briefly catalogue the quantization literature that motivates the
champion-scale follow-up in \texttt{docs/F2\_PRE\_REG.md}.


\subsection{ML ablation methodology}\label{sec:9.1}


\textbf{ABLATOR} (Fostiropoulos \& Itti, 2023) is the closest infrastructure
work: a tool for running multi-seed ablation studies at scale with
result aggregation. ABLATOR stops at multi-seed ranking; it does not
attempt mediation decomposition or stratified CDE analysis. F2 extends
the multi-seed-ranking workflow by adding causal-inference-grade
reasoning over the seeds.

\textbf{AblationBench} (Abramovich \& Chechik, 2025, \citep{arxiv:2507.08038})
provides a benchmark suite for the \emph{upstream} question of whether
language-model agents can plan the right ablations for a paper
(their best system identifies only 38\% of original ablations on
average). F2 is orthogonal to that question: given that the
ablation matrix is already chosen, we ask how to analyze the
resulting per-seed measurements without misattributing effects to
mediator-confounded knobs.

\textbf{Inferential reproducibility} (Hagmann, Meier \& Riezler, 2023,
\citep{arxiv:2302.04054}, "Towards Inferential Reproducibility of Machine
Learning Research") motivates the seed-stability discipline that F2
operationalizes. Hagmann et al. argue that seed nondeterminism alone
can flip baseline-vs-SOTA orderings; F2's \texttt{f2\_provenance\_check} + lock
tests are direct responses to this concern at the framework level.

\textbf{Applicability survey} (\texttt{papers/case\_study\_published\_ablations.md}).
We survey nine recent transformer-architecture and training-recipe
ablation papers (NormFormer 2021, OPT 2022, Switch Transformer 2022,
Pythia 2023, Mamba 2023, Llama 2023, BitNet b1.58 2024, Peri-LN
2025, plus the nanoGPT educational codebase) and find that the
multi-seed-with-data-release norm is not yet established in this
literature: \textbf{seven of nine publish single-run ablation tables},
\textbf{two report multi-seed summaries without per-seed CSVs}
(Peri-LN at N=5, Switch Transformer at N=3), and \textbf{zero release per-seed data alongside their ablation tables}. F2 can be applied
as-is to long-form CSVs with the contract in \cref{sec:3.5.1}; the case
study illustrates what F2 \emph{would} surface against the Peri-LN
Table 1 ablation if per-seed data were available, and explicitly
catalogues the methodological gap F2 is designed to close.


\subsection{Causal mediation}\label{sec:9.2}


The four-path decomposition we use in \cref{sec:3.2} is primarily attributed
to \textbf{Daniel, De Stavola, Cousens \& Vansteelandt} (2015, \emph{Biometrics}
71:1-14, doi:10.1111/biom.12248) as the foundational two-mediator
nested-counterfactual identification, with the no-interaction
reduction supplied by \textbf{Gao, Li \& Luo} (2020, \citep{arxiv:2007.16031},
"Decomposition of the Total Effect for Two Mediators: A Natural
Counterfactual Interaction Effect Framework"). Earlier drafts of this
paper mis-attributed the decomposition to "Zhao-Luo"; that attribution
was corrected to Daniel et al. (primary) + Gao-Li-Luo (no-interaction
collapse) in a follow-up validation pass.

The delta-method linearization we use to derive per-PSE SEs is in the
spirit of the \textbf{efficient-influence-function} treatment of Miles \&
Shpitser (2017, \citep{arxiv:1710.02011}). Their \cref{sec:3} derives the EIF for a
single-pathway PSE in the presence of mediator-outcome confounding;
we adapt the linearization logic to our two-mediator no-interaction
decomposition. We do not claim algebraic equality with their EIF ---
the lock test \texttt{dual\_mediation\_no\_interaction\_residual\_lock} (\cref{sec:8.2})
certifies only the Daniel et al. residual closure, not equivalence
to the Miles-Shpitser single-pathway EIF.

\textbf{DoWhy} (Sharma \& Kıcıman, 2020, \citep{arxiv:2011.04216}) is the closest
Python-side toolkit; we adopt its flat-record-per-estimate JSON
convention for \texttt{f2\_to\_jsonl} output. \textbf{CMAverse} (Shi, Liao, Aerts \&
VanderWeele, available via CRAN) is the R-side reference; we adopt its
long-form CSV convention for sensitivity sweeps. Neither toolkit
implements the Pearl-CDE-style stratum pinning that F2's mediator-
stratified sweep modes provide.


\subsection{Sensitivity analysis}\label{sec:9.3}


The \textbf{E-value} convention (VanderWeele \& Ding, Annals of Internal
Medicine, 2017, "Sensitivity Analysis in Observational Research:
Introducing the E-Value") motivates the \texttt{Γ\_tip} classification scheme
we adopt for fragility/robustness reporting in \cref{sec:3.3} and \cref{sec:5.4}. As we
note in \cref{sec:3.3}, the specific \texttt{Γ < 1.25} / \texttt{Γ >= 2.0} bracket boundaries
are a reporting convenience rather than literature-prescribed cutoffs;
the E-value paper itself does not prescribe universal thresholds, and
we do not claim it does.

The \textbf{bridge-score additive envelope} in \cref{sec:3.3} is from Ohnishi \& Li
(2026, \citep{arxiv:2605.18724}) Theorem 2. We use the additive scale (their
Eq. 6) directly; BPB is on the additive scale by construction, so no
log/risk-ratio translation is required.

The most recent sensitivity-analysis paper in our adjacent literature
is \textbf{Guo et al. (2026)}, "Sensitivity Analysis for Unmeasured
Confounding in Causal Mediation Analysis With Survival Outcome",
\emph{Statistics in Medicine} 45 (2026), doi:10.1002/sim.70548. They
extend mediation sensitivity analysis to survival outcomes without the
rare-outcome assumption that has constrained prior work, and address
both mediator-outcome and exposure-confounder confounding by simulating
the unmeasured confounder from its conditional distribution. Their
exposure-confounding axis is conceptually adjacent to our \cref{sec:3.3}
bridge-score \texttt{Γ} parameter; their setting (epidemiology / survival)
does not overlap with ML ablation, but a future stat-journal-grade
extension of F2 would borrow their conditional-distribution simulation
in place of the additive bridge-score.

We are not aware of prior work that combines E-value-style robustness
classification with mediator stratification, four-path decomposition,
and reproducibility-grade infrastructure in a single framework. The
F2 contribution is the integration plus the headline empirical
demonstration.


\subsection{Quantization (motivation for the champion-scale follow-up)}\label{sec:9.4}


The original research question that motivated this framework
(\texttt{Issue \#1021}) was a head-to-head BPB comparison between a phi-ladder
quantization path (GFTernary $\to$ GF8 $\to$ GF16 $\to$ GF32) and the mainstream
format-zoo (BitNet b1.58, INT4, FP8, bf16). The methodology work in
this paper was a by-product of preparing the analysis tooling for that
comparison; the comparison itself is deferred to the pre-registered
follow-up in \texttt{docs/F2\_PRE\_REG.md}.

For context on the format-zoo competitors, the key references are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{BitNet b1.58} (Ma et al., 2024, \citep{arxiv:2402.17764}, "The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits"), establishing the ternary \texttt{\{−1, 0, +1\}} weights baseline; and the follow-up \textbf{BitNet b1.58 2B4T Technical Report} (Microsoft, 2025, \citep{arxiv:2504.12285}) demonstrating the recipe at 2B params on 4T tokens.
\item \textbf{Quantization scaling laws}, partially addressed in QuEST (Panferov et al., 2025, \citep{arxiv:2502.05003}) --- a QAT method that characterizes the precision-vs-scale frontier as a side effect of proposing a new training recipe; we cite it loosely as the closest available proxy for a dedicated scaling-law treatment.
\item \textbf{FP8 at production scale}, see the published NVIDIA Nemotron MXFP8 recipe reports. We previously also cited InfiR2 (\citep{arxiv:2509.22536}) here, but that paper was withdrawn by its authors on 2025-10-17 due to a data-processing pipeline bug invalidating the reported results; we keep the citation for historical context only.
\item \textbf{NVFP4} (NVIDIA et al., 2025, \citep{arxiv:2509.25149}, "Pretraining Large Language Models with NVFP4") is the direct successor to the MXFP8 recipe above. It introduces a final-layers-in-BF16 hybrid. NVIDIA's paper does not claim this hybrid as a Pearl-style mediator decomposition; we cite NVFP4 because the BF16/FP4 split is exactly the kind of recipe-level heterogeneity that motivates the \cref{sec:3.1} stratification mechanism for \emph{future} (post-F2) champion-scale ablations, not because NVFP4 itself validates F2.
